dailyBrief.text: Good morning, Smileys — and an extra hour of morning, since the clocks fell back overnight. It's a cloudy, mild Sunday in Solon, high near 68°, and the overnight sports split the house: the Cavs rolled 136–111 in Milwaukee behind Mobley and Allen, while Ohio State fell 30–18 at USC with freshman Luke Fahey starting for the injured Julian Sayin. Overseas, Iran claimed tankers hit mines in the Strait of Hormuz — a story Washington calls false and Iran's own Guards deny — with oil holding near $117. Today is stacked: the Browns play at Pittsburgh at 1 PM for first place in the AFC North, and it is the final day of early voting, 1 to 5 PM at the Cuyahoga County Board of Elections, before Tuesday's midterms. And the biggest story of all is still your own — after last night's trip to the hospital, everyone here is thinking of Kelly and the baby.

weekBrief.text: The week ahead in Solon starts mild and turns wet: cloudy and about 63° Monday, the warmest day of the week Tuesday at about 73° for Election Day, then showers build Wednesday, rain is likely Thursday, and a sharp cooldown drops Friday into the low 50s. Election week frames everything — early voting ends today at 5 PM, polls are open Tuesday 6:30 AM to 7:30 PM (66 Cuyahoga precincts have moved, so check yours), and the governor's and Senate races top a long ballot. In sports, the Browns play at Pittsburgh today for first place, the Cavs — fresh off a 136–111 rout in Milwaukee — host Oklahoma City Monday night, and Ohio State looks to regroup after Saturday's loss at USC. The standout deal remains Giant Eagle's BOGO-free sirloin tip roasts through Wednesday — and at home, with Kelly's labor starting last night, this is the week the Smiley family very likely grows by one.

items.title: Cavs vs Oklahoma City Thunder
Iran's supreme leader orders a maximum response, with no geographic limits, to any new U.S. attack
items.summary:
Iran's supreme leader, Mojtaba Khamenei, has told his top military commanders that any renewed American or Israeli attack must be answered immediately and effectively, without geographic limits. The order came at the first publicly disclosed meeting between Khamenei and all three of his senior commanders since the war began, and he directed them to update Iran's target list so that American and Israeli assets of every kind fall within range.

The commanders at the table were Armed Forces Chief of Staff Ali Abdollahi, Army Commander Amir Hatami and Revolutionary Guards Commander Ahmad Vahidi. They briefed the leader on readiness along the Persian Gulf coast, in the Strait of Hormuz and the Gulf of Oman, and on Iran's other borders, and said weapons production and ammunition stockpiles have grown several-fold. Another senior security figure, Mohsen Rezaei, reinforced the message with talk of devastating blows and new weaponry.

The timing is pointed. The statement landed just after a Qatari mediation team held more than twelve hours of talks in Tehran and then continued in Doha, and Tehran has warned that strikes on its energy facilities would bring retaliation against oil and gas sites across the Gulf states. One American official told Axios that a heavy Republican defeat in Tuesday's midterms could raise the odds of a large new U.S. operation, which Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is urging to begin right after the vote.

Watch whether the Qatari channel produces even a small confidence step — one proposal would let U.N. inspectors back into bombed nuclear sites in exchange for some sanctions relief — or whether the threats become the story instead.

items.title: Russian strikes cut power to hundreds of thousands in Ukraine, while Ukrainian drones damage a big Russian refinery region
items.summary:
Russia attacked power infrastructure in four Ukrainian regions overnight, cutting electricity to hundreds of thousands of households, President Volodymyr Zelensky said Sunday. Ukraine's air force said it shot down 371 of 433 long-range drones Russia launched from Saturday evening, and Kyiv alone sounded six drone alerts after midnight.

Ukraine hit back at scale. Russia's Defense Ministry said it downed 235 Ukrainian drones overnight, and in the Nizhny Novgorod region the governor acknowledged significant damage to an industrial facility he did not name — the region hosts the NORSI refinery at Kstovo, one of Russia's largest, where a blaze was reported. Local officials urged drivers to buy fuel only as needed and avoid panic buying, and Zelensky said Ukrainian forces also struck the Kamensky plant in Rostov, which he said produces Russian missiles.

The exchange shows both sides now treating energy as a central battlefield: Russia is trying to deepen Ukraine's power deficit heading into winter, while Ukraine is trying to make the war felt in Russian fuel supplies and prices. Russia's deputy prime minister for energy, Alexander Novak, conceded Sunday that the refinery strikes are adding to imbalances in global fuel markets.

Watch whether the power cuts in Ukraine stretch into rolling blackouts this week, and whether gasoline limits spread beyond the Nizhny Novgorod area.

items.title: A rare ceasefire in Kherson expires Sunday evening, and civilians are bracing for the war to come back
items.summary:
A localized ceasefire in Ukraine's Kherson region — described by the Associated Press as the most significant truce since Russia's full-scale invasion four and a half years ago — is set to end Sunday evening. The pause, which the White House says First Lady Melania Trump helped broker, began early Tuesday and allowed a rare joint evacuation operation.

The truce let residents of Russian-occupied Oleshky, on the left bank of the Dnipro River, get out before fighting resumes. About 2,000 civilians, including roughly 50 children, were in the town when the pause took hold, and evacuees could choose Ukrainian- or Russian-controlled territory, or stay behind with fresh food and medical supplies. The evacuation wrapped up Saturday.

Local officials warn that Russian forces used the quiet to bring in more weapons and personnel, and residents expect shelling to intensify. Fighting never fully stopped elsewhere in Ukraine during the truce — a Russian drone hit a vocational school in Vinnytsia, killing two people and injuring three, including young children.

Watch for any last-minute word of an extension. As of Sunday, neither Moscow nor Kyiv had announced one.

items.title: Riot police guard Poland's top court as the government moves to prosecute its two senior judges
items.summary:
Poland's fight over its Constitutional Tribunal escalated sharply, with riot police deployed at the court in Warsaw to keep demonstrators out and the justice minister moving to strip the tribunal's president and vice-president of their immunity so they can face criminal charges.

Justice Minister Waldemar Zurek says President Bogdan Swieczkowski and Vice-President Bartlomiej Sochanski should be charged over blocking newly elected judges from taking their seats. The tribunal answered that the two men remain its lawful leaders and called the actions against them a coup d'etat. Prime Minister Donald Tusk defended the push as restoring the rule of law after years of what he called lawlessness under the previous Law and Justice government, while President Karol Nawrocki, backed by that party, turned back from a trip to Senegal as the standoff deepened.

The dispute reaches back to 2015, when Law and Justice began appointing tribunal judges; European courts later ruled some were improperly seated and that the tribunal was no longer independent. Judge Anna Korwin-Piotrowska — one of five parliament-elected judges Nawrocki has refused to swear in — has now been placed in temporary charge of the court.

Watch whether prosecutors actually file charges, and whether European institutions weigh in again on which side of the court is legitimate.

items.title: Trump says the U.S. still has one or two Iran targets left, including Pickaxe Mountain, but he is in no hurry
items.summary:
Speaking to reporters at a Halloween party at Mar-a-Lago on Saturday, President Trump said the United States has already knocked out Iran's nuclear program but still has, in his words, one or two sites to take care of — naming Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected underground nuclear complex Iran insists hosts no nuclear work. He said the remaining sites could be handled in ten minutes.

At the same time, Trump downplayed urgency. He said negotiations to end the war are going fine while calling the Iranian side not very reliable, said he is not in a hurry either to strike again or to sign a deal, and refused to say whether action could come this week. Secretary of State Marco Rubio added that no final decision on further strikes has been made and that Washington remains open to a diplomatic outcome.

The remarks put the two tracks side by side days before the midterms: a standing military threat aimed at Iran's most sensitive remaining site, and a negotiating track in which mediators have floated a quick sequence to reopen the Strait of Hormuz in exchange for sanctions relief and released funds.

Watch Trump's first comments after Tuesday's vote — officials on both sides are treating the election result as a factor in what happens next.

items.title: Trump says Brazil's defeated Flavio Bolsonaro can stay in the U.S. as long as he wants
items.summary:
President Trump said Saturday evening that Brazilian Senator Flavio Bolsonaro, who lost Brazil's presidential runoff a week ago to incumbent Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, can remain in the United States as long as he wants. Trump called the election a disgrace and said Bolsonaro was treated very shabbily, though he said he has no plans to meet with him.

Bolsonaro arrived in Miami on Wednesday, days after a Brazilian Supreme Court justice revoked his passport. He faces two federal money-laundering investigations in Brazil, police considered him a flight risk, and he was admitted to the U.S. under humanitarian parole, a status that typically lasts one year. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who spoke with Brazil's top diplomat Saturday, insisted the administration did not help Bolsonaro flee.

Bolsonaro has refused to concede and has called the results fraudulent without providing evidence; his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro, is in prison in Brazil for plotting a coup after his own 2022 defeat. U.S. officials told Reuters Trump has no current plans to back the younger Bolsonaro's political ambitions.

The episode is likely to keep relations strained between the two largest democracies in the Americas, and Brazil's embassy in Washington had not responded to requests for comment.

items.title: A judge throws out Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal over the Epstein letter — for good
items.summary:
A federal judge in Miami has dismissed President Trump's $10 billion lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal, Rupert Murdoch and other defendants, and dismissed it with prejudice, meaning it cannot be refiled. U.S. District Judge Darrin Gayles said the president was grasping at straws and had tried to manufacture flaws in the Journal's reporting.

The case grew out of a July 2025 Journal story about a sexually suggestive letter bearing Trump's name in a 2003 album Ghislaine Maxwell compiled for Jeffrey Epstein's 50th birthday. Trump denied writing the letter and sued days later, claiming overwhelming harm. Under the Supreme Court's New York Times v. Sullivan standard, he had to show the paper acted with actual malice — knowledge of falsity or reckless disregard for the truth — and Gayles ruled the amended complaint fell short, calling its malice allegations conclusory and vague. The judge also noted the Journal's story itself reported Trump's denial that the letter was his.

This was the second time Gayles dismissed the suit; the first dismissal came in April, and Trump was allowed to refile in May. An appeal to the 11th Circuit remains possible, but the district-court case is over.

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Watch whether Trump appeals or lets the ruling stand in the middle of midterm week.

items.title: Ted Cruz warns Republicans could lose up to eight Senate seats — and every statewide race in Texas
items.summary:
Senator Ted Cruz used his own podcast Friday to deliver a blunt warning to his party: eight to ten Senate races are basically tied, and on a bad night Republicans could fall from 53 seats to 45. He went further on his home state, saying Republicans could lose Texas — not just the Senate race, but every single statewide contest.

Cruz blamed turnout. He said Democrats are massively out-turning-out Republicans in early voting, and that if only the early votes cast so far were counted, Republicans would lose both the House and the Senate in what he called a bloodbath. In Texas, Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton faces Democratic state Rep. James Talarico; a CNN/SSRS poll of likely voters in late October put Talarico ahead 49% to 43%.

Republicans have not lost a Texas statewide race in decades, and Texas last sent a Democrat to the Senate in 1988, which is what makes a warning like this, from Cruz, notable two days before the election. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take the Senate.

Watch whether Republican turnout surges on Election Day itself, which is the pattern Cruz's warning assumes his party needs.

items.title: Forecasters shift a dozen-plus races toward Democrats as Trump's approval hits an 80-year pre-midterm low
items.summary:
The Cook Political Report moved more than a dozen congressional races toward Democrats on Friday, and its latest picture has more than 220 House races favoring the party. If Democrats won everything they are favored in plus the toss-ups, they would hold around 240 seats — what would be their largest House majority in over a decade. They need 218.

The shift comes alongside grim numbers for the president. The New York Times polling average puts Trump's approval at 36% against 61% disapproval, and USA Today reports that is the lowest standing for any president heading into a midterm in 80 years — since Harry Truman, whose party was shellacked in 1946. In the final Times/Siena survey, under 3 in 10 likely voters backed Trump's handling of the cost of living, and more than 4 in 10 Republicans disliked how he has handled fuel costs.

The movement is showing up in money as well as ratings: a major Republican House fund reportedly cut millions in ad spending in two districts it had been defending. The current House stands at 218 Republicans to 214 Democrats, so even a modest swing flips control.

Watch the seven Senate toss-ups Cook counts, including Ohio and Michigan — Democrats need to win at least four of them to take that chamber too.

items.title: Democratic leaders head into Tuesday confident and paranoid, with a 9-point generic-ballot lead
items.summary:
Democrats enter the final days of the midterms with a 9-point lead over Republicans on the generic congressional ballot in CNN's Poll of Polls, and internal numbers described to CNN have party leaders already smiling about how the campaign is ending — while bracing for a long, close election night.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries spent Saturday campaigning in Virginia for Elaine Luria, trying to win back a district she flipped in 2018 and lost in 2022, then flew to Alabama to defend a seat targeted after a Supreme Court decision weakened the Voting Rights Act. Rep. Suzan DelBene, who runs the House Democrats' campaign arm, summed up the mood as confident and paranoid: confident about netting the seats needed for a majority, paranoid about ways the president might try to interfere with results.

Other Democrats see a broader shift among voters who backed Trump in 2024 on promises of lower prices and fewer foreign wars. Cleveland Mayor Justin Bibb, voting early, warned his party not to waste the moment: people, he said, need to see their pocketbooks improve, not just hearings.

One caution running through the piece: Rep. Bobby Scott predicts at least 20 races will be so close that the loser still gets 49% — a recipe for disputes that outlast election night.

items.title: A Michigan Democratic feud spills into the open as Haley Stevens shows up at church with the Republican nominee
items.summary:
Michigan's Democratic Senate primary ended in August, but the feud from it erupted in public on Sunday. Rep. Haley Stevens, who lost that primary to Abdul El-Sayed by less than a point, attended Sunday service at Detroit's Perfecting Church alongside Republican nominee Mike Rogers — separately entering the prominent Black church — instead of appearing with El-Sayed as planned.

The unity event, arranged with help from Reps. Debbie Dingell and Jim Clyburn, collapsed after Stevens demanded El-Sayed condemn an outside group's ad that blamed high grocery prices on U.S. aid to Israel. El-Sayed answered that Stevens seemed intent on relitigating a primary that ended three months ago, and his campaign told her to stay away from its events for the rest of the race.

The stakes are national: Michigan's open Senate seat is a must-win for Democrats' path to a majority, and the RealClearPolitics average gives El-Sayed a 3.5-point lead over Rogers with two days to go. Stevens' own fiance told Fox News he intends to vote for Rogers.

Watch whether party elders can patch this up before Tuesday — or whether the split becomes a story Republicans use in the final 48 hours.

items.title: OpenAI is preparing a post-midterm push to reshape the AI debate in Washington
items.summary:
OpenAI plans to launch a policy and public-relations campaign immediately after Tuesday's midterm elections, according to Axios, aiming to reset how Washington talks about artificial intelligence just as a likely Democratic House takes shape. The push would begin in the lame-duck session that opens November 9.

The company, led on this effort by global affairs chief Chris Lehane, has been stockpiling proposals since August. Its centerpiece is mandatory safeguards — speed limits — for the most powerful AI systems, designed to keep humans in control. OpenAI also wants to rebrand data centers as AI compute campuses, back state laws giving communities a say in how projects get built, and strike community agreements around new sites. Meta is separately working to strengthen its own ties with Democrats.

The backdrop is a backlash that has turned data centers into a local political fight in much of the country, including Ohio, where OpenAI's Stargate project in Pike County is planned at roughly 8 gigawatts. Both companies are also looking past this election to the 2028 presidential field, which starts forming the day after the midterms.

Watch for the first concrete proposal after November 9 — and whether lawmakers of either party pick it up or push back.

items.title: OpenAI cuts its fundraising target to $20 billion as big investors cool on AI
items.summary:
OpenAI has cut the size of the funding round it is trying to close from about $30 billion to $20 billion, and trimmed its target valuation from $1.4 trillion to $1.25 trillion, according to reporting by the Financial Times, The Wall Street Journal and CNBC summarized by TipRanks. The Journal reported roughly $11 billion secured so far, with some large investors responding tepidly or shrinking their allocations ahead of Friday's deadline.

Investors from the United Arab Emirates, including the state-backed fund MGX, are expected to lead what does close, alongside firms like Coatue, Founders Fund, Sequoia and Andreessen Horowitz. Even the reduced first close is expected to fall short of $20 billion, with a later offering to wealthy individuals possibly topping it up. OpenAI did not comment, and the round remains open.

The timing is not a coincidence: the cut landed as the Nasdaq 100 fell 3.46% on Friday in a broad AI selloff, and OpenAI is racing rival Anthropic, which is preparing an IPO at a reported valuation target of at least $1.5 trillion. An internal document cited in the reporting projects a cumulative free-cash-flow deficit of about $278 billion between 2026 and 2030, against more than $1.4 trillion in compute and data-center commitments.

Watch the final close figure — it will be read as a market verdict on how much of the AI buildout investors are still willing to fund.

items.title: Big Tech is returning the smallest share of its cash to shareholders in 15 years — the AI buildout is eating it all
items.summary:
Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle returned just 9.3% of their operating cash to shareholders as dividends and buybacks in the first nine months of 2026, down from 27.4% a year earlier and the smallest share in at least 15 years, according to a Reuters analysis. Capital spending is the reason: it doubled to $556.9 billion, more than the $542.9 billion the five companies' operations generated — a first in data going back to 2011.

The combined result is a free-cash-flow deficit of $14 billion, versus a $143.5 billion surplus a year ago. Buybacks were cut 83%, to $13.6 billion; Alphabet and Meta repurchased no shares at all in 2026 after buying back $66.5 billion worth in the same period last year. Amazon spent $75.9 billion on capital projects in the third quarter alone and raised $48.1 billion in long-term debt to help cover it.

For investors, this changes what owning these stocks means. The steady buyback bid that lifted earnings per share for years — Alphabet had shrunk its share count 9.5% from 2020 to 2025 — has paused, and with tech now about 43.5% of the U.S. market's value, the shareholder yield on the sector has fallen to a fraction of the rest of the market's.

Watch fourth-quarter guidance: any hint of slower capital spending would likely move these shares more than earnings themselves.

items.title: OPEC+ is set to hold oil output steady for December, with the Iran war still snarling exports
items.summary:
Seven core OPEC+ members have agreed in principle to keep oil production targets unchanged for December, three sources told Reuters, with the group's online meeting held Sunday. The members involved are Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan and Oman.

The decision extends a pattern: targets were also held steady for October and November after the group finished unwinding a 1.65 million barrel-per-day cut in September, and a separate layer of cuts of about 2 million barrels a day runs through the end of 2026. In practice, most members are pumping well below their targets anyway, because the U.S.–Iran war keeps disrupting Gulf exports.

That is why a no-change decision still matters for prices. With Brent crude near $117 a barrel and the Strait of Hormuz largely closed to normal traffic, there is little spare supply the group can actually deliver, whatever the targets say.

Watch the group's fourth-quarter review of each member's production capacity — it sets the baselines for 2027 quotas, and the arguments over them are where the real fight will be.

items.title: Qatar's stock market jumps 4.6% in its best day in eight years while the rest of the Gulf slides
items.summary:
Gulf stock markets mostly fell in Sunday trading as investors weighed the risk that President Trump resumes military action against Iran after the midterms — but Qatar broke sharply the other way. Its benchmark index rose 4.6% to 9,575, its biggest intraday gain in more than eight years, while Saudi Arabia's index slipped 0.8% and Egypt's fell 1.9%.

Two things supported Qatar. S&P affirmed the country's AA sovereign rating with a stable outlook, pointing to deep liquid, fiscal and external reserves. And QatarEnergy has been working to secure long-term liquefied natural gas supplies from the United States and other producers, which would protect the country's revenues if its own exports through the Strait of Hormuz stay disrupted. Qatar National Bank rose 3% and Industries Qatar, which is tied to QatarEnergy, jumped 7.9%.

Elsewhere the mood was defensive: Kuwait, Bahrain and Oman all eased, and in Saudi Arabia most stocks fell, including a 7.3% drop for developer Jabal Omar after it posted a quarterly loss.

The split captures the region's divide — countries with cash buffers and workarounds for the Hormuz closure are holding up, while the broader market is still pricing war risk first.

items.title: The AI buildout is hitting a physical wall: more than 300 local data-center moratoriums across the U.S.
items.summary:
The roughly $10 trillion race to build AI data centers is running into local resistance and plain physics, Axios reports: more than 300 local moratoriums now block data-center development around the country, as towns push back on power demand, water use and construction traffic.

The friction is not stopping the buildout so much as distorting it. Industry analysts at SemiAnalysis still project 50 gigawatts of new capacity in 2027, with half already in advanced construction, and developers have signed about $1 trillion in active leases. But in New York, an executive order pausing environmental permits is delaying nearly a gigawatt of capacity; in Texas, a governor-ordered audit is slowing grid connections; and in New Mexico, Oracle restructured protections around its $165 billion Project Jupiter over delay risks.

The bottleneck has shifted from computer chips to electricity and transmission — there is not enough power, in the places developers want it, as fast as they want it. Some investors now argue 25 gigawatts is a far more realistic 2027 figure than 50.

For Ohio, which has both giant projects planned and its own wave of local moratoriums, this fight will decide where the next round of campuses actually lands.

items.title: Early voting passes 50.5 million and beats the entire 2022 midterm turnout — with days still to go
items.summary:
More than 50.5 million Americans had voted early by Saturday morning in this year's midterms, according to the University of Florida Election Lab — nearly 5 million more than voted early in the whole 2022 cycle, with three days still left. By Saturday afternoon the running total had climbed past 51.3 million, at a pace of roughly 4 to 5 million ballots a day.

Texas leads the country with more than 7 million early votes; in Harris County, turnout passed 862,000 by Wednesday, compared with about 564,500 at the same point in 2022. In states that track party registration, 10.7 million registered Democrats and 7.8 million registered Republicans had voted — a measure of who has turned out, not how they voted. Turnout versus 2022 is up sharply in several states, including South Carolina, Maine, Kansas and Michigan.

Analysts caution that early-vote totals measure participation, not outcomes: both parties have banked millions of votes, and Election Day turnout on Tuesday will still decide most close races. On the ballot are all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 39 governorships.

Watch the final early-vote tally Monday, and whether Tuesday's in-person turnout keeps the record pace or falls off.

items.title: Chepkirui and Almgren win the New York City Marathon, and an American ends an eight-year podium drought
items.summary:
Kenya's Sheila Chepkirui won her second New York City Marathon title in three years on Sunday, finishing in 2:24:36 in a sprint through Central Park. On the men's side, Sweden's Andreas Almgren won in 2:06:01 in his marathon debut — the first Swede ever to win New York, and the first debut winner since 2010.

The loudest cheers were for second place in the women's race. Jessica McClain of Scottsdale, Arizona, overtook defending champion Hellen Obiri in the final meters to finish in 2:24:42, just 0.41 seconds ahead — the first American woman on the New York podium since Shalane Flanagan in 2018. The finish also automatically qualified McClain for the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. Italy's Yemaneberhan Crippa was second in the men's race and Lesotho's Kamohelo Mofolo third, on his 21st birthday.

Nearly 60,000 runners — the most ever — took part on the 50th anniversary of the five-borough course, watched by an estimated 2 million spectators. In the wheelchair races, Switzerland's Marcel Hug won his eighth New York title and compatriot Catherine Debrunner won the women's race by more than eight minutes.

The race was the last World Marathon Major of 2026 and the first day of the qualifying window for the 2028 Olympic marathon.

items.title: HealthCare.gov open enrollment starts today: premiums up about 13–15%, fewer insurers, and the subsidy cliff is back
items.summary:
Open enrollment for 2027 health coverage through HealthCare.gov opened Sunday and runs through January 15, with a December 15 deadline for coverage starting January 1. Shoppers will find a thinner, pricier market: the median proposed premium increase is about 15%, and KFF puts the average increase for the benchmark Silver plan at 13%, after a roughly 30% jump last year.

The bigger change is who gets help paying. The enhanced premium tax credits that lowered costs during and after the pandemic expired at the end of 2025 and Congress has not renewed them, so the old subsidy cliff is back — households earning above 400% of the federal poverty level no longer qualify for credits at all. At the same time, 11 insurers are leaving the market for 2027, including Cigna exiting all 11 states where it sells individual plans, and the maximum out-of-pocket limit rises to $12,000 for an individual and $24,000 for a family.

The effects are already visible: paid marketplace enrollment fell by about 2.6 million people, to 19.2 million, by February of this year. A few states, including Virginia and Rhode Island, are adding their own subsidies to soften the loss of federal aid.

Anyone who relies on a marketplace plan should shop rather than auto-renew this year — the plan that was cheapest in 2026 may not be in 2027, and missing the December 15 deadline means a February start.

items.title: A cross-country storm will soak 35 states this week — flash floods and evacuations in the Southwest today, snow in Colorado tonight
items.summary:
A powerful El Nino-fueled storm system is crossing the country and will eventually bring rain, severe thunderstorms or snow to more than 35 states. The worst of it today is in the Four Corners region, where forecasters put more than 65,000 square miles — an area the size of Washington state, home to over 4 million people — under a Level 3 of 4 flash flood risk.

Mandatory evacuations are in effect for parts of Sedona, Arizona, where Oak Creek is rising fast, and for homes in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, where the San Juan River is forecast to crest at 19.71 feet — above its all-time record of 17.8 feet — under a rare particularly dangerous situation flood warning. Up to 5 inches of rain could fall from Phoenix to Flagstaff through Monday. In Colorado's San Juan Mountains, the rain turns to 12 to 18 inches of snow Sunday night into Monday, making travel dangerous.

The system then moves east: Monday brings a severe-weather risk to Kansas, Oklahoma and northern Texas, and rain is expected across the central United States and parts of the South on Election Day, reaching the East Coast late in the week.

If you are traveling west or through the southern Plains in the next two days, check local warnings before setting out — flash flooding in desert terrain can close roads with little notice.

items.title: The Justice Department appeals the order blocking it from pressuring election officials — the order stays in place through mid-November
items.summary:
The Justice Department on Saturday appealed a federal judge's emergency order that bars it and the Department of Homeland Security from threatening election officials over how they process ballots. The order itself remains in force until November 16, with a hearing on a longer injunction set for November 13.

U.S. District Judge Trina Thompson issued the restraining order Friday in a suit brought by the SEIU, AFSCME, the League of United Latin American Citizens and the NAACP. While it stands, the administration cannot demand that officials segregate ballots, purge voters or halt ballot processing based solely on its claims that a registered voter is ineligible, and cannot threaten officials with prosecution for following state law. The judge wrote that the pressure campaign was likely to interfere with election administration and disenfranchise lawful voters.

The fight traces to letters the Justice Department sent to 29 states and Washington, D.C., threatening investigations and demanding voter data, built in part on Homeland Security data-matching lists that officials acknowledge are unreliable and include U.S. citizens. Separately, the 9th Circuit rejected a related administration effort in California to set aside thousands of ballots.

The appeal guarantees the legal fight runs past Election Day — meaning Tuesday's count will happen under the restraining order, whatever the appeals court eventually decides.

items.title: Ohio's early vote passes 1.59 million and breaks the state record on the final day of early voting
items.summary:
Ohio's early vote has already broken the state record for a midterm. Sherrod Brown's campaign, citing statewide totals as of Saturday night, said 1,595,206 Ohioans had cast ballots — comfortably past the roughly 1.39 million early votes that set the record in 2022 — and today is only the final day of early in-person voting, from 1 to 5 p.m. statewide.

Brown is running against Senator Jon Husted in one of the Senate races both parties are watching, and his campaign says it is tracking county-level early-vote data live to aim its final turnout pushes. Election Day is Tuesday, with polls open 6:30 a.m. to 7:30 p.m.

One rule deserves attention this year: under Ohio's new law, a mail ballot must be received by 7:30 p.m. on Election Day to count. A ballot still in the mail on Tuesday night will not count, so anyone holding one is better off delivering it in person.

The record pace fits the national picture — more than 50 million early votes nationwide — and it means a large share of Ohio's verdict is already locked in before Tuesday.

items.title: Ramaswamy pulls the attack ad featuring Amy Acton's mother after polling shows it backfired
items.summary:
Vivek Ramaswamy's campaign for Ohio governor has stopped running the attack ad that featured his opponent Amy Acton's estranged mother calling her daughter a lifelong liar. Ramaswamy said the ad had run to completion and that the campaign had moved on to other commercials; he did not apologize for it.

The ad appears to have hurt its sponsor. A Republican-commissioned poll reported by Axios, taken October 23–26 among 800 likely voters, put Acton ahead 50% to 42% — a wider lead than the 47% to 45% she held before the ad began airing on October 19. Eighty-six percent of voters had heard of the ad, and by two to one, those familiar with it said it made them more likely to support Acton. Governor Mike DeWine, a fellow Republican, called the ad deeply troubling and urged that it be withdrawn; the campaign had pledged $4 million behind it, though ad-tracking firm AdImpact says only about $1 million was actually spent.

Acton's campaign called the spot despicable and said it should never have aired. A separate Suffolk/USA Today poll of Ohio voters also had Acton in front, 48% to 44%, with the Libertarian candidate near 4%.

With Election Day on Tuesday, the episode is a reminder that the most memorable ad of a race is not always the one that helps — and both campaigns are now in pure turnout mode.

items.title: Ohio measles cases climb to 296 across 24 counties — nearly six times all of last year
items.summary:
Ohio has recorded 296 measles cases in 24 counties so far in 2026, according to the Ohio Department of Health — a 557% increase over the 45 cases in all of 2025. The state added 36 new cases in the past week alone, and the newest surge has shifted south: Pike County reported 20 new cases, in Ohio's third separate measles outbreak of the year.

Northeast Ohio still carries the largest totals: Geauga County has 54 cases, Ashtabula 47, Wayne 45 and Medina 27, while Cuyahoga County has just 3. Akron Children's Hospital has also flagged a possible exposure at its main hospital building on October 20. State health officials say the vast majority of cases are in unvaccinated people, and patients range from 15 months to 20 years old.

Ohio is part of a national picture: the United States has recorded 4,730 measles cases this year, the highest annual total since 1991. Ohio's kindergarten vaccination rate for the MMR shot has slipped below the 95% level experts cite for herd immunity, after years in which the state counted only a handful of cases annually.

Health officials urge families to check vaccination records — two doses of MMR are the standard protection — and to call ahead before visiting a doctor or hospital if measles symptoms appear, so other patients are not exposed.

items.title: A judge put Glenville back in the football playoffs — then University School refused to play the game
items.summary:
Cleveland Glenville's football season now depends on a courtroom. The Ohio High School Athletic Association removed the Tarblooders from the playoffs on Thursday after an audit found that many Glenville players — students at Ginn Academy, a magnet school with no sports of its own — had been incorrectly assigned to Glenville by the Cleveland school district. On Friday, Cuyahoga County Judge Andrew Santoli granted a temporary restraining order putting Glenville back in.

The association said it stands by its ruling but would comply with the court, and tried to reschedule Glenville's game against University School for Saturday at noon. University School refused, saying it would not compete in the rescheduled contest and would instead prepare to play Salem on Friday, which is where the bracket goes next either way.

Glenville is 8-2 and the No. 5 seed in its region, with three state championships in its history, including last year's Division IV title. This is the second time the school has been punished over the same assignment issue — it drew a $5,000 fine and three years' probation in 2018.

A hearing is scheduled for Monday, November 2. Until then, nobody in that corner of the bracket knows who is playing whom on Friday.

items.title: Cleveland unveils its new lakefront plan, and the $285 million first phase is heading out to bid
items.summary:
Cleveland has released its updated plan for the 50 acres of lakefront now occupied by Huntington Bank Field and waterfront parking lots, drawn up by Rotterdam firm MVRDV with DLR Group. The stadium, built in 1999, would be demolished by 2032 as the Browns' new covered stadium rises in Brook Park, and the land becomes a downtown extension of parks, streets, housing and shops along the water.

The first phase, at about $285 million, went to a pre-bid meeting this past week. It would convert the Shoreway into a boulevard and build a land bridge over the tracks and roadway, with construction possibly starting by the end of next year. The money in hand includes the $100 million Haslam settlement from the stadium deal and more than $150 million in federal and state grants; a second phase, from East 9th Street to the Innerbelt Curve, waits on further construction funding.

The vision includes a continuous waterfront promenade, a central park on the stadium's field footprint, and a sheltered central plaza designed to work in winter — an acknowledgment that a Cleveland lakefront has to be built for all seasons. Brecksville-based DiGeronimo Development is the master developer.

The full build-out is a six-phase, roughly 20-year project, so this week's bidding is the starting gun rather than the finish line — but it is the first piece with real money and a real schedule attached.

items.title: Ohio spent $1.17 billion on private-school vouchers last year — and the program's fate is headed to the state Supreme Court
items.summary:
Ohio paid out $1.173 billion through its five private-school scholarship programs in fiscal 2026, according to state education data — the second straight year over $1 billion, up from $610 million just three years earlier. The largest piece is EdChoice Expansion at $532.8 million for more than 105,000 scholarships, followed by traditional EdChoice at $284.6 million and the Cleveland Scholarship at $55.09 million for more than 8,000 students.

The money is flowing while the program's legality is in doubt. On October 15, a three-judge appeals panel unanimously ruled EdChoice unconstitutional, saying it violates the state constitution's promise of a thorough and efficient system of common schools — but the court stayed its own ruling, so scholarships continue uninterrupted. The state says it will appeal to the Ohio Supreme Court, with a filing expected around November 30 and a decision likely at least a year away.

The enrollment backdrop: public school enrollment in Ohio slipped to about 1.63 million students last year, while nonpublic enrollment rose to about 185,600.

For families using a voucher now, nothing changes this school year or next — but the Supreme Court case will decide whether the fastest-growing line in Ohio's education budget survives at all.

baby.tip: For the first hours after birth, skin-to-skin contact is the main event: baby on a parent's chest helps regulate the baby's temperature, breathing and blood sugar, and it is something Mike can do too, not just Kelly. Keep the hospital bag's long phone charger within reach, drink water whenever it's offered, and let the nurses set the pace — resting while the baby rests starts now, not at home.
baby.fact: A newborn's stomach is tiny — about the size of a cherry on day one, holding roughly a teaspoon or two at a time. That is why brand-new babies feed so often, and why frequent small feeds in the first days are exactly right rather than a sign something is wrong.
baby.fun: Today's tiny prep mission, hospital edition: start the notes-app list neither of you will remember later — first song played for the baby, the weather outside (cloudy and in the upper 60s in Solon), and one line about how each of you is feeling. Future you will be very glad past you bothered.
